title: Integrated Select Transactions Review
description: Combine the major Module 3 topics in an integrated CPA-style review.
html:
Integrated Select Transactions Review

This lesson brings together the major rules from FAR Module 3 and focuses on recognizing which accounting treatment applies to different transactions.

1. Accounting Changes & Errors

Change in Accounting Principle Generally Retrospective
Change in Accounting Estimate Prospective
Change in Reporting Entity Generally Retrospective
Material Prior-Period Error Correct Prior Periods
Quick Test:

New information usually points toward a change in estimate. Incorrect use or omission of information that was already available may indicate an error.

2. Contingencies

Probable + Reasonably Estimable → Accrue Reasonably Possible → Generally Disclose Remote → Generally Neither

If a probable loss is estimated within a range and no amount is a better estimate than another, the minimum amount in the range is generally accrued.

3. Revenue Recognition

Step 1 Identify Contract Step 2 Identify Performance Obligations Step 3 Determine Transaction Price Step 4 Allocate Transaction Price Step 5 Recognize Revenue When / As Performance Obligations Are Satisfied
Remember:

Receiving cash does not automatically mean revenue has been earned.

4. Principal vs. Agent

Principal Generally Reports Gross Revenue
Agent Generally Reports Fee / Commission

5. Deferred Taxes

Future Taxable Amount → Deferred Tax Liability Future Deductible Amount → Deferred Tax Asset Permanent Difference → No Deferred Tax

Deferred tax assets and liabilities are measured using enacted tax rates expected to apply when the temporary differences reverse.

6. Valuation Allowance

If it is more likely than not that some or all of a deferred tax asset will not be realized, a valuation allowance reduces the amount expected to be realized.

Gross DTA − Valuation Allowance = Net DTA

7. Fair Value Hierarchy

Level 1 Identical Items in Active Markets
Level 2 Other Observable Inputs
Level 3 Unobservable Inputs

Fair value is generally a market-based exit-price measurement.

8. Lessee Accounting

Lease Liability = Present Value of Lease Payments

The initial ROU asset generally starts with the lease liability and is adjusted for items such as prepayments, lease incentives, and qualifying initial direct costs.

Finance Lease Interest + Amortization
Operating Lease Generally Single Lease Expense

9. Subsequent Events

Condition Existed at Year-End → Adjust Condition Arose After Year-End → Generally Do Not Adjust → Disclose if Material

10. Integrated Example

Scenario

Assume Falcon Corp. is preparing its December 31 financial statements.

Before the statements are issued:

  • A customer declares bankruptcy because of financial problems that existed before December 31.
  • Falcon signs a new lease beginning next year.
  • A lawsuit existing at December 31 is determined to have a probable and reasonably estimable loss.
  • Falcon receives cash in advance for services it will provide next year.

Analyze Each Item

Customer Bankruptcy Adjust Year-End Receivable
New Future Lease Analyze Based on Commencement
Probable Estimable Lawsuit Accrue Loss / Liability
Advance Customer Payment Contract Liability Until Earned

Module 3 Master Memory Sheet

PRINCIPLE → Retrospective ESTIMATE → Prospective PROBABLE + ESTIMABLE LOSS → Accrue CASH BEFORE PERFORMANCE → Contract Liability FUTURE TAXABLE → DTL FUTURE DEDUCTIBLE → DTA LEVEL 1 → Active Market + Identical LEASE LIABILITY → PV of Lease Payments EXISTING YEAR-END CONDITION → Adjust Subsequent Event

Module 3 Key Takeaways

  • Identify whether accounting changes require retrospective or prospective treatment.
  • Determine whether contingencies require accrual, disclosure, or neither.
  • Apply the five-step revenue model.
  • Distinguish principals from agents.
  • Distinguish DTAs from DTLs and understand valuation allowances.
  • Know Levels 1, 2, and 3 of the fair value hierarchy.
  • Understand ROU assets and lease liabilities.
  • Determine whether subsequent events require adjustment or disclosure.

quiz.prompt: Before year-end financial statements are issued, a company learns that a lawsuit existing at year-end will probably result in a $300,000 loss, and the amount can be reasonably estimated. What is the appropriate general treatment?

choices.text: Disclose the lawsuit but recognize no loss
Wait until the lawsuit is paid
Record the amount as a deferred tax liability

quiz.explanation: A loss contingency that is probable and reasonably estimable is generally accrued. Therefore, the company recognizes a $300,000 loss and related liability.

objectives: Explain integrated select transactions review and its underlying principles.
Apply the topic to a financial-reporting scenario.
Evaluate common errors and their financial-statement effects.
